questions.q:
The bulb of an apparatus for testing electrical conduction will glow when the electrodes are placed in :

(i) Dilute hydrochloric acid
(ii) Dilute sulphuric acid
(iii) Glucose solution
(iv) Alcohol
questions.solution:
A solution conducts electricity only if it contains **free ions** to carry the charge.

**(i) Dilute hydrochloric acid.** HCl is a strong acid; in water it ionises completely :

$$\text{HCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{Cl}^-$$

Plenty of ions — **conducts**.

**(ii) Dilute sulphuric acid.** Likewise a strong acid, giving $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ — **conducts**.

**(iii) Glucose solution.** Glucose dissolves but does **not** ionise. It stays as neutral $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$ molecules — no ions, so it does **not** conduct.

**(iv) Alcohol.** A covalent compound that does not produce ions in water — does **not** conduct.

So the bulb glows for **(i) and (ii)** only.

The point of the question is that dissolving is not the same as ionising: both glucose and HCl dissolve freely, but only one of them releases ions.

questions.q: When a dilute acid reacts with a metal, the gas evolved is:
questions.solution:
**Hydrogen**, and it is tested with a burning splint: it burns with a **pop** sound.

$\text{Zn} + \text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} \to \text{ZnSO}_{4} + \text{H}_{2}$

questions.q: The reaction between an acid and a base to give salt and water is called:
questions.solution:
**Neutralisation**: $\text{Acid} + \text{Base} \to \text{Salt} + \text{Water}$.

$\text{NaOH} + \text{HCl} \to \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

It is exothermic, which is why an antacid tablet gives quick relief and why mixing strong acid and alkali warms the beaker.

questions.q: The formula of plaster of Paris is:
questions.solution:
Plaster of Paris is $\mathbf{\text{CaSO}_{4}\cdot\tfrac12\text{H}_{2}\text{O}}$ — one water molecule shared between two formula units, which is why the half appears.

It is made by heating gypsum ($\text{CaSO}_{4}\cdot2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$) to $373$ K, and it sets back to gypsum when mixed with water.

questions.q: Which of these turns red litmus blue?
questions.solution:
**Soap solution** is basic, and a base turns red litmus **blue**.

The other three are acidic (citric, acetic and lactic acid respectively) and would leave red litmus red.

questions.q: A solution has a hydrogen ion concentration of $10^{-5}$ mol/L. Find its pH.
If a solution has pH $9$, find its pOH.
Find the molar mass of washing soda, $\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}\cdot10\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, in g/mol. (Na $= 23$, C $= 12$, O $= 16$, H $= 1$.)
questions.solution:
$\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3} = 46 + 12 + 48 = 106$.

$10\text{H}_{2}\text{O} = 10 \times 18 = 180$.

Total $= 106 + 180 = \mathbf{286}$ g/mol — most of it is water of crystallisation.

questions.q: How many water molecules of crystallisation are present in blue vitriol (copper sulphate crystals)?
questions.solution:
$\text{CuSO}_{4}\cdot5\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ — $\mathbf{5}$.

Heating drives them off and the blue crystals turn **white**; adding water restores the blue, which is the standard test for water.

questions.q: How many times more acidic is a solution of pH $3$ than one of pH $6$?
questions.solution:
Each pH unit is a factor of $10$ in $[\text{H}^{+}]$, and the difference is $3$ units.

$10^{3} = \mathbf{1000}$ times more acidic.

The scale is logarithmic, which is why small-looking pH changes matter so much — a pH drop of $0.5$ in a lake is a serious event.

questions.q: Give four examples of the importance of pH in everyday life.
questions.solution:
1. **In our bodies.** The stomach makes hydrochloric acid at about pH $1.2$ to digest food. Too much causes acidity, treated with a mild base — an **antacid** such as magnesium hydroxide.

2. **Tooth decay.** Bacteria in the mouth turn sugar into acid. Below **pH $5.5$** tooth enamel ($\text{Ca}_{5}(\text{PO}_{4})_{3}\text{OH}$, the hardest material in the body) begins to dissolve. Toothpaste is basic and neutralises it.

3. **Soil and crops.** Plants grow well only in a narrow pH range. Acidic soil is treated with **quicklime or chalk**; alkaline soil with organic matter or gypsum.

4. **Acid rain and aquatic life.** Rain below pH $5.6$ runs into rivers and lakes. Below about pH $5.6$ fish cannot survive, so a whole lake can be sterilised by rain falling hundreds of miles away.

5. **Stings.** A bee sting injects an acid, soothed by baking soda; a nettle sting also injects methanoic acid, and dock leaf sap is the traditional remedy.

questions.q: What is the chlor-alkali process? Write the equation and name the three products with one use each.
questions.solution:
**The process.** Electricity is passed through **brine**, a concentrated solution of sodium chloride:

$2\text{NaCl} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \to 2\text{NaOH} + \text{Cl}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}$

It is called chlor-alkali because the two main products are **chlor**ine and the **alkali** sodium hydroxide.

**Products and where they go:**

• **Chlorine** — at the anode. Used for water treatment, PVC, and bleaching powder.

• **Hydrogen** — at the cathode. Used as a fuel, in margarine, and for making ammonia.

• **Sodium hydroxide** — in the solution. Used for soaps and detergents, paper making, and degreasing metals.

The products are also combined again: chlorine with dry slaked lime gives **bleaching powder** ($\text{CaOCl}_{2}$), and with sodium hydroxide gives household bleach.

It is an unusually economical industry — everything that comes out of the cell is worth selling.

questions.q: Describe the preparation, properties and uses of (a) baking soda and (b) bleaching powder.
questions.solution:
**(a) Baking soda, $\text{NaHCO}_{3}$.**

*Preparation:* $\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2} + \text{NH}_{3} \to \text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl} + \text{NaHCO}_{3}$

*Properties:* a mild, non-corrosive base. On heating,

$2\text{NaHCO}_{3} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} \text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2}$

*Uses:* in **baking powder** (with tartaric acid, whose job is to neutralise the sodium carbonate left behind — otherwise the cake would taste bitter); as an antacid; in soda-acid fire extinguishers.

The carbon dioxide released is what makes bread and cake rise.

**(b) Bleaching powder, $\text{CaOCl}_{2}$.**

*Preparation:* $\text{Ca(OH)}_{2} + \text{Cl}_{2} \to \text{CaOCl}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

*Properties:* a pale yellow powder smelling strongly of chlorine, which it releases slowly on standing in air.

*Uses:* bleaching cotton, linen and wood pulp; **disinfecting drinking water**; and as an oxidising agent in industry.

Note that dry slaked lime is used, not a solution — with water the reaction takes a different course.

questions.q: Distinguish between a strong and a weak acid, with two examples of each, and describe how you would tell them apart in the laboratory.
questions.solution:
**Strong acid** — ionises **completely** in water, giving many $\text{H}^{+}$ ions. *Examples: HCl, $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$, $\text{HNO}_{3}$.*

**Weak acid** — ionises only **partly**, so most molecules stay intact. *Examples: acetic acid (vinegar), carbonic acid, citric acid.*

**Telling them apart** (at the **same concentration**, which matters — a dilute strong acid can have a higher pH than a concentrated weak one):

1. **pH / universal indicator** — the strong acid gives a much lower pH (about 1) than the weak (about 3–4).

2. **Reaction with magnesium or carbonate** — the strong acid fizzes vigorously, the weak one slowly.

3. **Electrical conductivity** — the strong acid conducts far better, because it has more ions. This is the most direct test, since it measures the ions themselves.

**Strong is not the same as concentrated.** Strength is about how completely the acid ionises; concentration is about how much of it is in the water.

questions.q: What happens when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to sodium carbonate? Write the equation and describe the test for the gas evolved.
questions.solution:
**Reaction.** Brisk effervescence — a gas is given off quickly:

$\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3} + 2\text{HCl} \to 2\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2}\uparrow$

**Test for the gas.** Pass it through **limewater** (calcium hydroxide solution). It turns **milky**:

$\text{Ca(OH)}_{2} + \text{CO}_{2} \to \text{CaCO}_{3}\downarrow + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

**A second stage worth knowing.** Pass excess gas through and the milkiness **disappears**, as the insoluble carbonate becomes soluble bicarbonate:

$\text{CaCO}_{3} + \text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \to \text{Ca(HCO}_{3})_{2}$

This same pair of reactions builds stalactites in limestone caves — dissolving on the way down, depositing again as the gas escapes.
